comments.text:
Opus decision (2026-11-07, claude-opus-5-5):

# fx-aw6 decision (Opus, 2026-11-07; scratch, never commit)

## Decision

**D3's lossless rule applies to address casts. Under the `unsafe` grant an
address, a raw pointer's or a function pointer's, counts as a `usize`, so a
cast between an address and an integer is lossless exactly when the matching
`usize` cast is under reference 4.2.** Lossy address casts are `FX0301`. A
cast between raw pointer types, or from a reference to a raw pointer, keeps
the address and is accepted, even when it drops a slice's length (as
`cast()` does). Without the grant, every address cast stays `FX0520`
(unchanged). This is Codex's option 2, done more cheaply than the memo
priced it: no new width or signedness rules, because 4.2 already defines
them for `usize`.

Accepted under the grant: `p as usize`, `p as u64`, `p as u128`,
`p as i128`, `f as usize`; `n as *const T` for `n` a `usize`, `u32`, `u16`,
or `u8`. `FX0301`: `p as u8`, `p as u32`, `p as isize`, `f as u32`, and
`n as *const T` for `n` a `u64`, `u128`, or any signed integer. The
spellings that remain: `u32::try_from(p.addr())`, `p.addr().truncate()`,
`usize::try_from(n)? as *const T`, `n.cast_unsigned() as *const T`.

Reasons:

- D3's rule exists to stop silent truncation, and a truncated address is the
  same bug as a truncated length (`p as u32` on a 64-bit target is a classic
  porting bug). A pointer-to-integer cast is safe Rust: the grant is what
  admits *observing* an address (GLOBAL-4, determinism), not what makes
  truncation intended. Nothing about unsafe code's trust hole makes `as`
  lossy on purpose.
- It adds a definition, not an exception: the learner applies the existing
  4.2 table with "address = `usize`". That is lower entropy than "`as` is
  lossless, except address casts", and costs one short sentence in 4.2.
- Every rejected form has an admitted, explicit spelling (`addr()` and 4.2's
  conversions), and the common Rust idioms (`p as usize`, `n as *const T`
  with `n: usize`) still work as Rust.
- It promises nothing about provenance or dereferenceability; GLOBAL-4 says
  so in one sentence, so "lossless" is not read as "valid".

Rejected:

- **Option 1, exempt address casts from D3 (the memo's recommendation).** Its
  argument ("the grant already admits address nondeterminism and unsafe code;
  preserving address bits cannot prove dereferenceability") is a non
  sequitur: D3 never claimed a cast proves validity, and D3 is about values,
  not trust. It also classifies a truncating cast as a trust hole, which it
  is not: a cast breaks no checker guarantee (RUN-4 lists the routes that
  do). It adds an exception to D3 and drops the protection where low-level
  code most needs it.
- **Option 3, named conversions only (reject pointer/integer `as`).** Rejects
  `p as usize`, the dominant Rust idiom, against "You know Rust. Write Rust";
  more reference text for no extra safety (exposed provenance is the same).
- **Option 4, strict provenance only.** Broader than the bead, costs interop
  and budget, and `transmute`/`asm!` under the same grant mean it buys no
  guarantee.
- **Gating pointer-to-pointer casts that drop metadata as lossy.** `cast()`
  does the same with a method name, so rejecting `as` there only moves the
  spelling.

Placement: D3 (01) owns the rule and its reason (01 owns every language
decision); GLOBAL-4 (03) elaborates which casts it accepts and the
provenance caveat, without restating the reason; `conformance/rules.md`'s
GLOBAL-4 row names `FX0301`; reference 4.2 gets the one-sentence rule and
reference 11's row gains the function pointer's address observers, which
the reference never mentioned.

Budget: the reference at base `d12d7e0` measures **25,019** tokens, over the
25,000 budget before this bead (the same counter gives 24,995 for `3cfb299`,
the companion's recorded count, so it is stable; fx-kw8.23's `db225c5` added

title: Implement sim.world.proc in tide-std's simulator and runtime
description:
## Why
Stage-3 prerequisite of the Tide-in-Eon ladder (epic, label eon-adoption). fx-f6xp designs sim.world.proc (child processes, signals and PTYs in the simulator). Eon's Runtime supervisor can't run under Tide's simulator until that design is implemented.

## Scope
Implement fx-f6xp's accepted design in tide-std's simulator and real runtime, with conformance cases and its replay-manifest identities (fx-nkv.7). Read Eon spike eon-vux87's outcome first.

## Acceptance
Implements design/03 §9.9 as fx-f6xp landed it (research/30 §7 and §8). Done when all of these hold:
- One supervisor fixture uses Proc, Child, Signals and Pty under both Linux and the simulator; model setup is the only test adapter. §1.1's Child wait, drop and cancellation rules stay observable. The library, the conformance stub, admission's classification of the handles, the conformance mapping and the docs agree.
- research/30 §8's contract matrix passes, and each deliberately broken control fails. The matrix covers spawn, exit vs signal death (exit 143 vs Term), per-Child wait ownership and cached status, signal subscription with AlreadyExists, coalescing and seeded order among latched signals, Winch and resize coalescing, Hup on master drop, parent-only death (SIGPIPE, survivors adopted and not inherited on restart, run_until's seed failure vs run_until_exit's status) vs node crash, proc_hold and proc_release, the polling stall guard, and Child::signal rejecting Kill.
- Every permitted finite outcome has a seed witness that records its model and fault plan. Outcomes that only fixed ties or holds reach have explicit `at` scenarios. Real checks use allowed sets and causal order with external watchdogs, never the simulator's PIDs, timings or counts.
- The existing scheduler handles process events without changing its time, cancellation or deadlock rules. Models, faults, inputs and versioned profile identities replay inline under fx-nkv.7 and REPLAY-1/2; a changed model or build identity is refused. No-host canaries cover spawn, signals and PTY operations, including absent models (a coverage failure that stops the seed, also under --allow-unmodeled) and stale targets.
- The first delivery is §9.9's bounded Linux profile, with explicit coverage failures for unsupported process modes; it is not the Eon adoption milestone. If the work is split into child beads (research/30 §7: lifecycle and signals; PTY on top of that; faults, manifest and reachability), the parent closes only after the full matrix passes.

title: Benchmark Tide's build time and compiler memory against plain cargo on the Eon fixture
description:
## Why
Stage-1 gates (b) and (c) of the Tide-in-Eon ladder (epic, label eon-adoption). Tide must not measurably slow Eon's builds or raise compiler memory. Eon's 2026-11-12 efficiency review already rejected tools that cost build time, and this machine OOM'd twice that night.

## Scope
A repeatable benchmark that compares the stage-0 fixture crate (fx-vjvb) built through tide-admit with the same crate built by plain cargo/rustc on Eon's pinned stable toolchain:
- full-workspace clean and incremental builds;
- the crate's own incremental rebuild;
- peak RSS per compiler or driver process.

Report medians of 5 or more runs in a booked quiet slot, on the same machine and Eon commit, through heavy.sh. Publish one result file per toolchain pin. No Eon edits.

## Acceptance
- One command reproduces the table.
- The stage-1 thresholds are evaluated and stated pass/fail:
  - workspace clean and incremental within +3%;
  - crate incremental within +10%;
  - peak RSS within +10%, never over the 6 GiB per-process cap (eon-os2bi).
- A failing gate gets a bead naming the cost's source.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Revision 3 of the ladder (fx-ho6o) supersedes this bead's measurement method.
- Run interleaved ABAB pairs. Report medians and CV; if CV is over 1%, raise N. Budget about 2 quiet slots per side, about 20 workspace builds; time one clean build first.
- Measure on x86_64-linux only.
- This bead owns the peak-RSS wrapper: RUSTC_WRAPPER, or systemd-run --scope with memory accounting, per rustc and per Tide driver process. Limits: within +10%, hard ceiling 6 GiB. The 6 GiB is eon-os2bi's target, not a heavy.sh cap.
- Book no quiet slots before Eon's v0.2.0 cut.

description:
## Why

§10.1 row E1-P6 (B1, B3–B7, B9). fx-o8o's map: B3 fails on fs::Mode, B4 on fs::OpenOptions, B6 on
fs::Mode. Production std's Fs has no operations. Part of epic fx-byk.

## Scope

Fs with every method design/reference.md §6.3 lists (read, read_to_string, write, exists, read_dir,
metadata, rename, remove_file, remove_dir, remove_dir_all, create_dir_all, write_synced, open,

Mode::Read rejects writes; append mode writes at the end; write_synced plus sync_dir follow §6.3;
a file operation in a cancelled scope returns ErrorKind::Cancelled; E1 tasks B3, B4 and B6 no longer
fail on fs::Mode or fs::OpenOptions. Toolchain tests prove each item executes, not only
type-checks. Std API changes must also satisfy fx-nkv acceptance on production/conformance
equivalence; the production library owns runtime behavior.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Design decisions 2026-11-10 (coordinator Opus, from Fable research /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/tide-research-files/report.md; the report lands in research/ as 19-files.md with fx-byk.1):
1. Confinement (03 §1.1's openat2 semantics): a real Fs holds base: Option<Arc<OwnedFd>> + Mode; dir() opens O_DIRECTORY|O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC through the parent and keeps the fd (the capability names the directory, not its path). Every op resolves with openat2(base, path, RESOLVE_BENEATH|RESOLVE_NO_MAGICLINKS) when confined, plain openat(AT_FDCWD) for root.fs. rename/unlink/rmdir/mkdir open the parent beneath the base (O_PATH|O_DIRECTORY) and act on a normal last component. EXDEV from the resolving call only -> PermissionDenied (renameat's stays CrossesDevices); absolute paths on a confined Fs rejected in Tide before the call; EAGAIN retried 4 times; ENOSYS -> Unsupported, fail closed, no lexical fallback. dir() returns Unsupported off Linux for now.
2. Dependency (AP-DEPENDENCY-001): rustix pinned exactly, default-features=false, features fs+std, plus one extern close() for File::close's result. Owned raw libc code (per-arch stat/dirent layouts) and cap-std (weight for platforms v0 doesn't target, second handle-type set) rejected. Replacement cost: one private backend module. Proof: the escape tests; record cargo tree -p tide_std.
3. One Fs/File/ReadDir/DirEntry type with a private Real/Sim enum (fx-byk.2 adds Sim); shared code in front of both backends: cancellation check, Mode::Read -> PermissionDenied before any writing op (and O_RDONLY as defence), path checks, File access-flag checks.
4. Paths: no lexical normalization on either side; byte-exact names; '.'/'..' as the last component of rename/remove_file/remove_dir -> InvalidInput (S2); write to a read-only File -> PermissionDenied in the shared wrapper (S3, departs from Rust's EBADF kind; record in 03); dir(p, ReadWrite) on a Read Fs -> PermissionDenied at dir() (S6).
5. Errors: ErrorKind is the contract; real errors via from_raw_os_error. read_dir reads the whole listing and returns entries sorted by name bytes (S1, provisional; each next() stays a checkpoint). Metadata: type and length only (S5). write_synced syncs the file then its parent dir.
6. Record S1-S12 as std behaviour in design/03 and the companion (reference.md is single-holder at 24,998/25,000 tokens: do not grow it).
Out of scope, reported only: 03 §2.6's seccomp list must admit openat2 or confined file access fails inside tide's sandbox (RUN-3's owner).

title: Simulated file system: sim.fs, sim.world.file, and real/simulated equivalence
description:
## Why

E1's file suites (B3, B4, B6, B7, B9; trials/e1-checked/suites/tide/fs.rs) run on `Root::sim(seed)`'s
`sim.fs`. design/reference.md §6.8: every capability has a deterministic simulated version;
`sim.world.file(path, contents)` creates a file and its parents; each file operation takes up to
1 ms of virtual time (provisional) and is a scheduling point. Part of epic fx-byk.

## Scope

The simulated file system behind SimRoot's fs field, implementing fx-byk.1's whole Fs, DirEntry and
File surface with the same paths, errors and confinement, sim.world.file, scheduling points through
fx-nkv.5's scheduler, and virtual time through fx-o8j. Crashes and fault injection stay out
(companion 17). Production std under crates/; no new language semantics. Protocol §2 held-out
rules apply.

## Acceptance

The same file program gives the same results on real and simulated roots (one test runs both);
sim.world.file creates parents; simulated file operations advance sim.elapsed() within §6.8's
bound; a fixed seed gives identical traces twice. Toolchain tests prove each item executes. Std API
changes must also satisfy fx-nkv acceptance on production/conformance equivalence.

Reviews r1-r3 Codex, r4-r5 Opus (all fixed; final approve). Workspace 158, conformance 257-19-0.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Design decisions 2026-11-10 (coordinator Opus, from Fable research /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/tide-research-files/report.md; see fx-byk.1's comment of the same date for the shared type, path and error rules):
1. Store: inode table, inodes: BTreeMap<InodeId, Inode> with simulation-local ids; File { data } / Dir { entries: BTreeMap<OsString, InodeId>, parent }; an inode lives while a name or open handle refers to it; one mutex never held across a scheduling point. Simulated base is an inode id. No symlinks/hard links in sim. Physical resolver over Path::components() with the kernel's rules (missing/../f -> NotFound; trailing slash on a file -> NotADirectory; empty -> NotFound; NUL -> InvalidInput; >255-byte component -> InvalidFilename); errors built from kinds (no raw OS code; documented).
2. Each simulated op (all Fs/File methods, ReadDir::next, DirEntry::metadata/file_type): cancellation check (Cancelled: no draw, no time, no effect) -> latency draw uniform 0..=1_000_000 ns from an fs sub-stream with its own domain constant -> block on fx-o8j's timer (the scheduling point; cancellation doesn't cut it short) -> apply the whole op under the store lock. One method call = one op = one draw. File::close: no cancel check, but one point and draw. sync/sync_dir/write_synced validate and take time, no durable/volatile split (crashes are companion 17's). One 'fs' trace event per op (step, task, op, span, path, latency, result); names provisional until fx-nkv.7.
3. sim.world.file(path, contents) -> (): from simulated /, creates parents, creates or replaces, immediate, no point/time/draw/Mode, panics on setup errors, records one 'world' trace event.
4. Equivalence: one suite of fn case(fs: &Fs) -> Vec<Observation> run on a real Fs confined to a fresh temp dir and on sim.fs.dir("/t", ReadWrite), asserting equal observations (values or ErrorKinds), covering every error-table row, append/seek/set_len, rename and handles outliving rename/remove, read_dir order, nested dir()/read_only(), '..' inside and out; run through tide-admit's build tests. Equivalence claimed for Linux, case-sensitive fs. Simulated multi-call ops apply whole (S4, recorded as a limit beside 03 §9.8).

## Why

On 2026-11-12 an uncapped Tide landing run overloaded the shared machine: load 44, and Lucca's computer went slow. eon-overseer's heavy-queue stopgap (lr8sx.21.1, "0T") asks that every Tide heavy run go through heavy.sh with caps. ## Decision

Lucca, 2026-11-12: "you decide". Coordinator decision: amend it.

## Scope

Edit `.agent-protocols.local.md`, a single-holder governance file, then render AGENTS.md from the pinned Starcompass source per BR_WORKFLOW and the apply-agent-protocols procedure. The new rule:

title: Decide the Pure status of std types that erase a Send + Sync payload (io::Error, Waker; owner decision)
description:
## Why

Std types that erase a `Send + Sync` payload have no stated `Pure` status,
which opens a determinism hole in v0 parallel regions. If `io::Error::new`
or `io::Error::other` is admitted with Rust's signature
(`E: Into<Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>>`) and `io::Error` is `Pure` (the
default reading, since 02 §9 does not list it), a user error type whose
`Display` runs `Shared::with` lets two `join` branches observe each other's
order: `join(|| e1.to_string(), || e2.to_string())` captures only
`&io::Error`, yet the shared log ends `[1, 2]` or `[2, 1]` by schedule, and
authority-free code runs a blocking lock. `core::task::Waker`, built safely
by `Waker::from(Arc<W>)` for `W: alloc::task::Wake` holding a `Sender`, is a
second route. Found by round 35 (N1) while reviewing fx-u18; it predates
fx-u18.

## Evidence

- `reviews/round35-consistency.md` N1: the full construction and both
  routes.
- `design/02-memory.md` §9: the deep rule "looks through every field,
  private ones included"; applied to std's own fields it would make `Vec`
  not `Pure` through its raw pointer, so std's types must take their status
  from the table, which names neither `io::Error` nor `Waker`.
- `design/02-memory.md` §9 "What std must provide in return": "No operation
  on a `Pure` type may return a result that depends on other tasks"
  implies `io::Error` cannot be `Pure` with an unbounded payload, but no
  text states the decision.
- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` ADMIT-1: the "at least" list names
  neither `core::task` nor `alloc::task::Wake`; D8 and reference 7 exclude
  only `async`, `Future`, `Pin`, and executors.
- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §3.3: "`Pure` arguments reach no
  capability or handle" fails here if `io::Error` is `Pure`.
- `design/reference.md` 92–94: std error types are `Send + Sync`.

## Decision needed (owner)

How is `io::Error`'s erased payload handled? Options: (a) bound the payload
of `io::Error::new` and `io::Error::other` by `Pure` (a Tide std signature
divergence; cheap, since `io::Error` appears in most `Result`s and stays
`Pure`); (b) classify `io::Error` as not `Pure` (breaks authority-free code
that returns `io::Result`); (c) another shape. Round 35 recommends (a).
Recommend before writing; this changes which programs check.

## Scope

In scope:
- the decision above, stated in 02 §9 and in the std signature text that
  owns `io::Error`;
- add `core::task` and `alloc::task::Wake` to ADMIT-1's "at least" list
  (`FX0520`), under D8, and to reference 6.9 if core tokens allow;
- one sentence in 02 §9: std's types take their `Pure` status from the
  table and their type arguments, not from a walk of std's private fields;
- an audit of std's other payload-erasing types (`Box<dyn Error + Send +
  Sync>` conversions, `Any` payloads such as panic payloads, and any `dyn`
  field in a std type) against the 02 §9 obligation, listing each verdict.

Out of scope:
- v1 imported crates (separate bead).
- Changing 01 D7 or D8 without asking.

## Acceptance

- 02 §9, 03 ADMIT-1 and §3.3, and the reference agree on `io::Error`'s and
  `Waker`'s status, and the round-35 construction no longer type-checks
  under the stated rules.
- The audit's list is recorded in the review or in 02.
- A review round in `reviews/` finds no contradiction and no new
  construction of the same shape.

## Implementation Notes

1. Ask the owner the decision first.
2. Find where Tide std's `io::Error` constructors are specified
   (`grep -rn "io::Error" design/`).
3. Docs-only: review rounds, not converge.

## Verification

- A fresh reviewer asked to rebuild round 35's N1 construction, or another
  through an erasing std type, cannot.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop and ask before changing 01 D7 or D8.
- The core reference is at 24,969 of D14's 25,000 tokens (companion "Core
  count" line); recount with `scripts/count-tokens.sh design/reference.md`
  and pay for any core addition with a cut, or put it in the companion.
close_reason: io::Error::new/other admit only alloc's four From impls (Pure error, String, &str, Cow<str>); std types walked with raw-pointer and erased-payload exceptions; fmt::Arguments/Formatter not Pure; core::task/alloc::task outside ADMIT-1. Opus rounds 36-38, 40-41; Codex rounds 39 (request_changes) and 42 (approve). Core 24,996 tokens.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Decision (agent, under AGENTS.md 'Decisions', 2026-10-20): (a) Tide std's io::Error::new and io::Error::other take E: Into<Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> + Pure, so io::Error stays Pure and io::Result, NetError, TaskError are unaffected. Rejected (b) io::Error not Pure: it would strip Pure from every error enum wrapping it and from authority-free code returning io::Result. core::task and alloc::task (Waker, Context, Wake) go outside ADMIT-1: they exist only for async (D8). Audit of std types that erase a payload: io::Error (bounded by Pure); Box/Rc/Arc<dyn Trait>, dyn Any, Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync> (not Pure by the dyn rule unless a Pure companion trait); fmt::Arguments (neither Send nor Sync, so no branch shares one); Waker/Context (not admitted); Panicked carries a String; TaskError, LockError, NetError, UrlError, Cancelled, json::Error hold data or io::Error. 02 §9 states std's types take their Pure status from the table and their type arguments, not a walk of std's private fields.

title: Define invalid-offset behavior for Ferox source locations and line index conversions
description: Ferox should define what happens when a requested offset falls in the middle of a multibyte codepoint, beyond file bounds, or on otherwise invalid boundaries. This task should settle whether invalid offsets are rejected, rounded, clamped, or reported structurally, and it should align parser, diagnostics, and tooling behavior on that choice.
design: Primary question: what should Ferox do when an offset is out of bounds or lands in the middle of a multibyte codepoint? Define invalid offset behavior for parser utilities, diagnostics rendering, line-index conversions, and future tooling APIs, including whether failures are structural errors, option-like absence, or explicit diagnostics-only behavior.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task defines invalid offset behavior for in-bounds non-boundary offsets, out-of-bounds offsets, empty files, and line-ending edge cases; aligns parser and diagnostics expectations; and includes examples showing why Ferox rejects silent rounding/clamping by default if that is the chosen model.
notes: Decision: keep this idea. Ferox should reject invalid offsets by default instead of silently rounding or clamping them. Offsets that are out of bounds or that land in the middle of a UTF-8 codepoint should be treated as invalid for source-location conversions and structured utility APIs. Safe conversion APIs should return explicit absence or structured failure; internal assertion-style helpers may panic in debug-only or clearly internal contexts, but machine-readable outputs and parser-facing helpers must not silently coerce to a nearby boundary. Rationale: this matches rust-analyzer's try_line_col/offset discipline and Rust's own char-boundary model, and it avoids hidden drift in diagnostics, formatting, and future tooling. Apply in v1 immediately as part of the bootstrap source-location contract, before T074/T075/T076 stabilize more offset conversions. This is a foundational behavior choice, not a later ergonomics feature. Follow-on work still needs to specify line-span variants and preservation-versus-normalization semantics before fx-e1i closes.

title: Reproduce Eon's historical supervisor races in Eon's ported supervisor under Tide's simulator
description:
## Why
Stage-3 gate (a) of the Tide-in-Eon ladder (epic, label eon-adoption). A hand-written model reproducing a race only proves the model (eon-desk, 2026-11-13), so the evidence must come from Eon's real supervisor code.

## Scope
Port Eon's Runtime supervisor lease and reap paths (runtime/crates/eon-runtime/src/supervisor.rs and what they need) at a pinned Eon commit into the stage-0 fixture as a Tide crate, with no Eon edits. Run it under Tide's simulator with sim.world.proc, Unix sockets (fx-ssek), planted faults (fx-m0f5) and replay manifests (fx-nkv.7). Use the fx-vjvb lease-race model only as a stepping stone.

## Acceptance
- At least 2 historical Eon races, eon-awmq.6 (reap) and eon-l4e7s (expired startup deadline), are reproduced in the ported code.
- Each is found within 1,000 seeds and replays deterministically from its seed.
- Each port edit is recorded and counted.

title: Later-tier review findings (v1 and Later)
description:
## Why

Owner decision, 2026-10-21: later-tier review findings no longer block or
restart a review loop. They are recorded here instead, so they are neither
lost nor fixed early. The rule lives in `GOVERNANCE.md`, "Merge Rule".

The test (GOVERNANCE.md): a finding blocks when its fix would change a tier
the change edits or an earlier one. It comes here only when its fix would
change later-tier text alone that the change does not edit. A v0 rule that
overreaches into a later-tier feature is a v0 defect and blocks: for example
`reviews/round96-consistency.md` B1, where TASK-3's abandonment rule caught
an in-process Bend kernel and the fix went into TASK-3.

Evidence for the change: since the Codex rule, beads took about 6 review
rounds each (fx-arx 14, fx-sz7 about 10).

## How to use

- A reviewer or author who meets a later-tier finding adds a comment here:
  the review round, the file and line, the tier, and the finding in a few
  lines. One comment per finding.
- This bead stays deferred. When v1 design work is scheduled, triage its
  comments into beads, then close it.

## Acceptance

- Every later-tier finding from a review round after 2026-10-21 appears here
  as a comment, or in a bead filed from one.

title: Define the Ferox source-text, span, and line-ending contract for diagnostics, parser, and tooling
description: The bootstrap code now uses UTF-8 Rust strings, byte spans, line-column mapping, and newline-sensitive source handling, but the spec does not yet define that contract explicitly. This task should define the Ferox source-text model for parser, diagnostics, formatter, and machine-readable outputs so later tooling does not accidentally diverge on encoding, span meaning, or line-ending treatment.
design: Primary question: what is the exact source-text and location contract Ferox uses across parser, diagnostics, and tooling? Define: 1. source file encoding assumptions; 2. whether primary spans are byte-based, character-based, or both; 3. how line and column data is derived; 4. what newline normalization or preservation rules apply; 5. how diagnostics JSON and formatter/source reproduction interact with this contract.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task clearly answers: Ferox source encoding assumptions; the authoritative span model; line and column derivation rules; newline handling; and validation/logging expectations. Include concrete examples for multibyte text and line endings, rejected alternative models, compatibility implications for diagnostics JSON, and corpus/e2e expectations for source mapping behavior.
notes: Synthesis decision: keep the overall source-text contract and apply it in v1 immediately. Ferox should use UTF-8 source text with byte offsets as the sole authoritative internal span unit, represented as half-open ranges over preserved original source text. Human-facing line/column data is derived from byte offsets rather than stored as competing primary coordinates. Invalid offsets, including offsets inside a multibyte codepoint or outside file bounds, should be rejected by safe conversion APIs rather than silently rounded or clamped. Ferox should explicitly model both line spans excluding trailing line breaks and line spans including them; the excluding-break form is the default logical line-content view, while the including-break form is used explicitly for physical-layout and formatter-sensitive operations. Full-fidelity source preservation and formatter normalization are separate layers: preserved source remains the ground truth for spans, recovery, and reproduction, while formatted output is a derived canonical rendering that may normalize layout and line endings without redefining the original source. This is a foundational v1 bootstrap contract that should be locked before T074/T075/T076 stabilize parser, formatter, diagnostics, or machine-readable source locations.

title: Close cancellation gaps: output/status orphan child, exists, owned-buffer errors, write counts
description:
## Why

The fx-ms8 reviews (rounds 95–97) found cancellation gaps that predate it:

1. A cancelled `Command::output()` or `status()` can orphan its child. Both are checkpoints that
   start a `Child` internally; cancelled after the spawn, the call drops the running `Child`, and
   the caller cannot `kill` or `wait` it. The Receivers note uses exactly this outcome to justify
   `wait_with_output`'s `&mut self`.
2. `Fs::exists` returns `bool` but is a checkpoint, so it has no error to carry a cancellation.
3. The error type of `read_owned` and `write_owned` is never named, so nothing says how the `Vec`
   comes back inside it (TASK-3).
4. A cancelled socket or pipe write may have reached the peer, but its error carries no byte count.
5. Core 7.2 says joins, scope exit, and `File::close` "are never interrupted" without saying that
   this makes cleanup deadlines soft (TASK-5); agents may treat them as hard.

## Evidence

- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §1.1 (Proc row, Receivers note, Owned buffers), TASK-3,
  TASK-5.
- `design/reference.md` 6.x (`Fs`), 7.2.
- `reviews/round95-consistency.md`, `round96-consistency.md`, `round97-consistency.md`
  (out-of-scope sections).

## Scope

In scope: decide each item in 03 (for example, `output`/`status` kill and reap the child before
returning a cancellation; `exists` under cancellation; name the owned-buffer error type; whether a
cancelled write reports a count), and state in the core only what fits D14's budget. Out of scope:
TASK-3's rules settled by fx-ms8.

## Acceptance

- 03 decides each item with reasoning; nothing in `design/` contradicts it.
- The core stays under D14's budget (recount with `scripts/count-tokens.sh`).
- A review round in `reviews/` finds no contradiction.

## Notes

Docs-only: review rounds, not converge. The core is at 24,996 of 25,000 tokens.

comments.text:
Decisions, 2026-10-21 (agent, per Decisions), in 03 §1.1, TASK-3, TASK-5, TASK-6:
1. A cancelled output()/status() whose child has started tries to kill it, closes its own ends of the child's pipes, waits for it to exit (shielded) even if the kill failed, and returns Cancelled; a failed kill (e.g. EPERM for a setuid child) is logged as warn!. Leaving the child running orphans it; returning the kill error drops the only handle; keeping pipe readers open can deadlock a surviving child (r2 B1).
2. Fs::exists -> io::Result<bool>, as std::fs::exists; Ok(false) only for NotFound.
3. read_owned/write_owned return Result<Vec<u8>, io::BufError>, after IntoInnerError's shape (error, into_error, into_inner, into_parts, From for io::Error) plus kind, is_cancelled, written; read_owned appends one read into spare capacity, write_owned writes all.
4. A cancellation error from a single write means no byte was accepted; accepted bytes return Ok(n). write_owned reports partial progress via BufError::written(); write_all keeps io::Result<()>, as in Rust.
5. Joins, scope exit, and uncancellable system calls make every deadline soft (TASK-5, TASK-6, core 7.2).
Also: conformance stub std's Fs::exists now returns io::Result<bool>. Core: 24,996 of 25,000 tokens (scripts/count-tokens.sh). Deferred for budget: naming BufError in core 2.2. Out of scope, not done: simulated short writes (r1 N2). For fx-djp: std-emitted warn! under SINK-9 (commented there).

title: std::io core in Tide's std: Read, Write, BufRead, BufReader, and io::Error
description:
## Why

fx-o8o's Tide-failure map (2026-11-07/08, trials/e1-checked/readiness.md): C10 fails on E0432 for
io::{BufRead, BufReader, Write}; B3 fails on E0425 io::Result; B4 on io::Write; and B3, B4, B6, B7
and B9 build io errors from io::ErrorKind (NotFound, InvalidInput, InvalidData) with `.into()`.
Production std's io module holds only Stdin. design/reference.md §1 keeps the std::io traits and
types (Read, Write, Seek, BufRead, BufReader, BufWriter, io::Error, io::ErrorKind, io::Result); §2.2
makes io::Error `Error + Send + Sync + Pure` with `io::Error::new`/`other` taking only a Pure error or
a string; §7.2 names `io::ErrorKind::Cancelled` as the cancellation kind; §6.9 keeps
`io::Error::last_os_error` FX0520. fx-byk (files), fx-hxw (TCP) and fx-5vj (stdin, stdout/stderr)
all need these types, so this bead owns them once (AP-OWNERSHIP-001) and those beads implement the
traits for their handles. Created per fx-o8o's Acceptance ('a missing owner gets a new prerequisite
bead linked to fx-ic2'); the owner approved creating beads (2026-11-07: 'creating is fine'). Widened
from BufRead/BufReader to the io core by the 2026-11-09 plan review.

## Scope

In production std (crates/tide-std): std::io's Read, Write, Seek and BufRead traits with Rust's
provided methods (read_line, lines, read_to_string, write_all, flush, ...), BufReader, BufWriter,
SeekFrom, io::Error with `From<ErrorKind>`, io::ErrorKind including a Cancelled kind, an
`is_cancelled()` test, io::Result, and impls over in-memory readers and writers (&[u8], Vec<u8>,
Cursor). Research, decide and record (on this bead and in design/03) whether these are Rust's
re-exports, as the conformance stub has them today, or Tide-owned types, given ErrorKind::Cancelled
and the Pure-only constructors; keep the stub and production equivalent. Admission-allowlist entries
for these items; `io::Error::last_os_error` stays FX0520. Out of scope: impls for File, TcpStream,
Stdin and stdout()/stderr() (fx-byk, fx-hxw, fx-5vj) and BufError/read_owned/write_owned (03).
No new language semantics. Protocol §2 held-out rules apply: no E1 code in tests or docs.

## Acceptance

A program that wraps an in-memory reader in BufReader, reads lines through BufRead, writes through
Write, builds an io::Error from an ErrorKind, and tests a Cancelled error with is_cancelled() passes
the driver's check and runs, through tide-admit with the production std. E1 tasks B3, B4 and C10 no
longer fail on E0425/E0432 for io::Result, io::Write, io::BufRead or io::BufReader. Toolchain tests
prove each item executes, not only type-checks. Std API changes must also satisfy fx-nkv acceptance
on production/conformance equivalence; the production library owns runtime behavior.

comments.text: Decision (fx-ecb, landed 2026-11-09): std::io's core types are Tide std's own, not Rust re-exports. Rust's ErrorKind cannot gain Cancelled, and its nearest kind, Interrupted, is one that Rust's read_exact, read_to_end and write_all retry, which would never end under level-triggered cancellation. So ErrorKind (Rust's stable kinds + Cancelled), io::Error (with is_cancelled()), io::Result, Read, Write, Seek, BufRead, their adapters, BufReader, BufWriter, IntoInnerError and io::prelude are Tide's, with Rust's API and behaviour except: BufWriter<W: Sized>; BufWriter's Drop does no I/O and discards unflushed bytes (TASK-6; the warn! is fx-5vj's); Lines, Split and Bytes end after yielding a cancellation error. Cursor and SeekFrom stay Rust's. new/other keep Rust's signatures and the FX0517 payload check is rekeyed to tide_std::io::Error::{new, other}; last_os_error is defined and denied (FX0520). Production and the conformance stub share crates/tide-std/src/io/shared.rs through include!. Recorded in design/03 §1.1 and reference §1. Builders fx-byk.1, fx-hxw and fx-5vj implement these traits for their handles; a Rust io::Error from an OS call becomes a Tide one through Error::from_raw_os_error(code) or a mapping they add to shared.rs.

title: Decide: trim the review loop after e32775f
description:
## Decision

Is `GOVERNANCE.md`'s review loop still worth its cost after `e32775f`, or
should named steps be trimmed?

Recommendation: measure first, then decide, once at least 5 beads have closed
under `e32775f`'s rules. Expected answer: keep the parallel first review and
the second-model rule, and trim the later confirmation and re-check rounds only
where the data shows they rarely change a result. This is the biggest lever on
how fast Tide moves autonomously. Record the decision here.

## Why

The review loop in `GOVERNANCE.md` is the main limit on how fast Tide lands
changes. `fx-djp` records about 6 review rounds per bead since the Codex rule,
with fx-arx at 14 and fx-sz7 at about 10. `reviews/` reached round 101 on
2026-10-21. Commit `e32775f` changed the loop to parallel first reviews and
tier-scoped blocking. Whether that is enough has not been measured.

## Evidence

- `GOVERNANCE.md`, "Merge Rule": the round sequence and the tier test.
- `fx-djp`: the per-bead round counts before `e32775f`.
- `reviews/round<N>-*.md`: one file per round, with its model, verdict, and
  blocking findings.

## Scope

In scope:
- A measurement over `reviews/` and `git log`: rounds per landed bead, and
  which rounds produced blocking findings that changed the result, before and
  after `e32775f`.
- A decision, recorded on this bead. Then either no change, or an amendment to
  `GOVERNANCE.md` and the overlay's "Governance" summary, rendered.

Out of scope:
- Removing the independent second-model review, or the rule that no change
  lands without a supervisor verdict. Both stay.
- Design documents.

## Acceptance

- This bead records the before and after numbers, with how they were counted.
- It records a decision, with its reasons: keep the loop, or change named
  steps. The decision cites the rounds whose findings justify each kept step.
- Any governance change keeps the two rules out of scope above, and is
  rendered with a clean drift check.

## Implementation Notes

1. Start only once at least 5 beads have closed under `e32775f`'s rules.
   Before that, comment with the current count and stop.
2. Count with a small script, not by hand, so the numbers can be rerun. Keep
   it in the bead comment, or in `scripts/` if it is reused.
3. Tide's "Decisions" rule makes this a technical decision for the agent.
   Report it to the owner, without asking first.

## Verification

- Rerunning the counting script should reproduce the recorded numbers.
- If governance changed, `starcompass check-consumer` should pass with the
  four Tide paths.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if fewer than 5 beads have closed under the `e32775f` rules.
- Stop if the data cannot separate rounds that changed a result from rounds
  that did not.

## Maintenance Notes

- The candidate trims are the later confirmation and re-check rounds. The
  parallel first review is the part to keep.
close_reason: Measured (comment has numbers and script): design changes fell from 7.0 to 4.2 reviews each after e32775f. Decision: keep the loop unchanged; the docs-only Codex re-check (clean 4/4) is the trim candidate, to recount after about 10 more docs-only changes.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Note, 2026-10-21: review files are now named per bead (GOVERNANCE.md, Merge Rule): <bead>-r<N>-opus.md and <bead>-r<N>-codex.md, with the first-round pair sharing N. Count review files under both schemes (round<N>-*.md mapped to beads through git log; <bead>-r<N>-*.md by name), and count Opus and Codex reviews separately rather than round numbers.

Count, 2026-10-21: 1 of the 5 beads needed have closed under e32775f's rules (commit time 04:29:15Z): fx-9ag (reviews/fx-9ag-r1-opus.md + r1-codex.md parallel pair, r2-opus, r3-codex; landed 76dfe06). fx-ms8 closed before it (04:07Z); review-names-r* (901c512) is not a bead. In progress under the new rules: fx-gcs.1, fx-e3t, fx-t99. Stop condition holds; not started. Recount from the repo root:

comments.text: Recount after a3b0177: 2 of 5 (fx-9ag; fx-t99, reviews fx-t99-r1-opus/r1-codex parallel, r2-opus, r3-codex: 4 reviews, no blocking finding in any; only r1 Opus's three wording nits changed text). Still at the stop condition.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Measurement and decision, 2026-10-21 (agent, per Decisions). Head 6f23e82.

Counted with the script at the end (run from the repo root). Each review file maps to a bead: reviews/round<N>-*.md through the subject of the commit that added it, reviews/<bead>-r<N>-<reviewer>.md by name. Only reviews added after 4a05cc7 (the Codex rule) count; "before" and "after" split at e32775f's commit time. A review blocks when its verdict asks for changes, or, for a converge round without a verdict, when it lists fixes it made. Sequences: o = Opus, c = Codex, ! = blocking.

Before e32775f (9 beads, all design): 7.0 reviews per bead, 59% blocking.
  fx-0ai o! o! o! o c! o c | fx-1am o! o! o! o c! o! o! o! c! o c | fx-arx o! o! o! o! o! o! o o c! o c! o! o c | fx-cze o! o! o c! o! o! c | fx-kdj o! o o c | fx-ms8 o! o! o! o c | fx-nyy o! o c | fx-obr o! o c! o c | fx-sz7 o! o! o! o c! o c
After (5 beads plus 2 bead-less governance changes): 6.3 reviews per change, 50% blocking.
  design: fx-9ag c o! o c | fx-e3t c! o o! o o c | fx-t99 c o o | governance (e32775f) o! c! o c | review-names c! o o c  -> 4.2 reviews per change
  code: fx-3md c! o! o! o o! o! o c! o! c | fx-gcs.1 c! o! o! o! o! o! o c! o! c o! o c  -> 11.5 reviews per change, mostly converge rounds that fixed something

Decision: keep the loop as GOVERNANCE.md states it; change no step now. The parallel first review cut design changes from 7.0 to 4.2 reviews. Each kept step has findings behind it:
- Parallel first Codex pass: blocked in round 1 on 5 of 7 changes (fx-3md, fx-e3t, fx-gcs.1, review-names r1, round100). Before, Codex blocked after Opus came clean on 6 of 9 beads (fx-0ai, fx-1am, fx-arx, fx-cze, fx-obr, fx-sz7), restarting the loop.
- Opus confirmation after fixes: fx-e3t r2 found a gap in the round-1 fix; fx-9ag r1 Opus found the Decisions conflict Codex approved past.
- Narrow Codex re-check: on code it blocked twice on real defects (fx-3md r7: a hand-started continuation could be launched twice; fx-gcs.1 r7). On design it came clean 4 of 4 (fx-9ag r3, fx-e3t r5, round102, review-names r3). That is the one trim candidate: skipping the re-check for docs-only changes. Four observations are too few to remove a second-model check, so it stays; recount when about 10 more docs-only changes have landed.
- Code converge rounds are the remaining cost (fx-gcs.1 13 reviews, fx-3md 10), but their late rounds kept finding real defects (fx-3md r4: commits touching only .beads/ reset the handoff stop; r5's lock finding; r6's untested prompt and log rules), so no trim there either.

Script:
"""Review cost per landed bead, before and after e32775f (fx-eit).

Run from the Tide repository root: python3 review_stats.py
Old files (reviews/round<N>-<kind>.md) map to the bead named in the subject of
the commit that added them; new files (reviews/<bead>-r<N>-<reviewer>.md) map
by name. Only beads whose reviews all postdate 4a05cc7 (the Codex rule) count.
A review is blocking when its verdict line asks for changes, or, for a
converge round (no verdict), when it lists fixes it made.
"""
import glob, os, re, subprocess, collections

def git(*a):
    return subprocess.run(['git', *a], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip()

codex_rule = int(git('log', '-1', '--format=%ct', '4a05cc7'))
cutover = int(git('log', '-1', '--format=%ct', 'e32775f'))

def verdict(path):
    lines = open(path).read().splitlines()
    for i, l in enumerate(lines):
        if re.match(r'^#+\s*verdict', l, re.I) or l.lower().startswith('**verdict'):
            rest = [x for x in lines[i:i + 4] if x.strip()][:2]
            v = ' '.join(rest).lower()
            return 'block' if re.search(r'request.?changes|changes needed|changes requested|revise|reject|with fixes', v) else 'clean'
    # A converge round has no verdict: it changed the result if it lists fixes.
    for i, l in enumerate(lines):
        if re.match(r'^##\s*(fixed|blocking fixes)', l, re.I):
            nxt = [x for x in lines[i + 1:] if x.strip()][:1]
            if nxt and re.match(r'^\s*([-*]|\d+\.|###)', nxt[0]):
                return 'block'
    return 'clean'

rows = collections.defaultdict(list)  # (era, bead) -> [(n, reviewer, verdict)]
for f in glob.glob('reviews/*.md'):
    name = os.path.basename(f)[:-3]
    added = git('log', '--diff-filter=A', '--format=%ct %s', '--', f).splitlines()
    if not added:
        continue
    t, subject = added[-1].split(' ', 1)
    t = int(t)
    if t < codex_rule:
        continue
    m = re.match(r'(.+)-r(\d+)-(opus|codex)$', name)
    if m:
        bead, n, who = m.group(1), int(m.group(2)), m.group(3)
    else:
        m = re.match(r'round(\d+)-(\w+)$', name)
        if not m:
            continue
        n, who = int(m.group(1)), ('codex' if m.group(2) == 'codex' else 'opus')
        b = re.findall(r'fx-[a-z0-9.]+', subject)
        bead = b[0] if b else 'governance'
    rows[('after' if t >= cutover else 'before', bead)].append((n, who, verdict(f)))

for era in ('before', 'after'):
    tot = collections.Counter()
    print(f'== {era} e32775f')
    print(f'{"bead":<18}{"reviews":>8}{"opus":>6}{"codex":>6}{"block":>6}  sequence')
    for (e, bead), rs in sorted(rows.items()):
        if e != era:
            continue
        rs.sort()
        c = collections.Counter(w for _, w, _ in rs)
        nb = sum(v == 'block' for *_, v in rs)
        seq = ' '.join(f'{w[0]}{"!" if v == "block" else ""}' for _, w, v in rs)
        print(f'{bead:<18}{len(rs):>8}{c["opus"]:>6}{c["codex"]:>6}{nb:>6}  {seq}')
        tot.update(beads=1, reviews=len(rs), opus=c['opus'], codex=c['codex'], block=nb)
    if tot['beads']:
        print(f'beads {tot["beads"]}, reviews/bead {tot["reviews"] / tot["beads"]:.1f}, '
              f'blocking share {tot["block"] / tot["reviews"]:.0%}')

title: Decide v0 contract details left open by the E1 dialect round: generated tests, private fields, while-loop invariants
description:
## Why

The held-out E1 round under D18 (trials/e1-dialect/, bead fx-jv9) used attribute contracts
correctly, which D18's reversal condition watches, but three contract-semantics questions are
undecided for v0, and ring's tests rested on two of them (grading.md C5, C6).

## Evidence

trials/e1-dialect/grading.md §5:
- G10: do generated tests over a type with private fields build it only from call sequences that
  respect each call's `requires` (discarding a violating call), and how are sizes such as
  `with_capacity(n)` drawn (04 §2.4 rule 1)? And fix the violation message prefix that
  `#[should_panic(expected = ..)]` matches (04 CLAUSE-7; reference 10.1 marks it provisional).
- G11: may a `pub` method's v0 clause read a private field (04 §1.4 is about v1 spec fns;
  reference 10.1's visibility rule is provisional)? The answer decides whether
  `self.len == old(self.len) + 1` is checked or must go through `len()` and be sampled
  (04 CLAUSE-5).
- G12: where `invariant!` runs in `while` and `while let` loops (01 D10 says only entry and exit;
  04 §2.4 fixes the next-index rule for `a..b` alone; the D18 spike checks before each evaluation
  of the condition).

## Scope

In scope: decide G10, G11, G12 in 04 (and 01 D10 if a decision changes it), then update
reference 10.1/10.2.

Out of scope: std and simulator details (the sibling bead for G3-G6, G9); v1 proof forms (fx-qzp).

## Acceptance

- 04 decides each item with its reasoning; reference 10.1/10.2 state the decisions and drop the
  matching "provisional" markers; the core stays under D14's budget (24,989 of 25,000 tokens;
  recount with scripts/count-tokens.sh).
- A review round in reviews/ finds no contradiction among 01, 04, and the reference pair.

## Implementation Notes

1. Check each decision against the D18 spike's contract lowering (spikes/d18/macros/) and say
   where it would change.
2. Docs-only design work: review rounds, not converge (GOVERNANCE.md).

## Verification

- The review file's verdict is approve or approve with notes.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop and ask the owner if a decision changes D10's v0 contract model.
close_reason: G10-G12 decided by the owner and written to 01 D10, 04, 02, and the reference; rounds 23-24 (approve with notes)

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Owner decisions (2026-10-20). G11: a v0 clause may name whatever the function body can name (private fields and functions included); v1's prove-time visibility (04 §1.4) applies only under prove. G10: generated call sequences evaluate each call's requires first and skip a call that fails it (the generator is the caller); scalars are full-range, biased to small and boundary values, so limits belong in requires; violation panics start 'requires violated: ', 'ensures violated: ', 'invariant violated: ' plus the clause text. G12: invariant! in while/while let is checked each time control reaches the condition, before evaluating it; the check before the failing evaluation is the exit check; a side effect of the failing condition is not checked (matches the D18 spike, for's next-index rule, Dafny). Baseline 557d4e5.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Owner decision (2026-10-20), consequence of G12: debug and test builds evaluate a checked invariant of a while/while let loop, and of a for over a general iterator, each time control reaches the loop head; for over a..b keeps entry and exit in debug builds; sampled invariants keep tide test's iteration schedule. D10 and CLAUSE-6 say so.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Closing. Decisions written to 01 D10, 04 (CLAUSE-2, -5, -6, -7, §1.4, §2.3, §2.4), 02 §7, reference 10.1/10.2. Reviews: round 23 changes requested (B1 reference debug-build wording, B2 spike differences), answered; round 24 approve with notes, notes answered. title: Decide whether Tide is a new language or a checked dialect of Rust
description:
Decide whether Tide ships as a new language (the current design) or as a checked dialect of Rust: every Tide program is valid Rust and compiles with rustc, and Tide adds a capability std, the simulator, and the trust diff.

Context:
- Draft 3.4 (af8a99c) adopted Rust's lifetime syntax, so the translation to Rust (design/02-memory.md §11) is the identity on lifetimes.
- research/12-newcomer-sweep.md (24cd216) records lust (https://github.com/t3dotgg/lust-lang): a checked subset of valid Rust whose warm daemon reports one-line body edits checked 60-250x faster than cargo check (cold about 2.5x; self-reported). Fast builds therefore no longer distinguish Tide. Its open question 7 states this question.
- The thesis in design/01-design.md says tools layered on Rust cannot give D7 (no ambient authority), D15 (deterministic simulation), and D11 (trust diff). That is shown for Rust as a whole, not for a checked subset with its own std.
- Owner decision (2026-10-19): settle this before planning v0 implementation. The handoff's plan to build the origin/borrow checker first depends on the answer: under a dialect, rustc checks borrows.

Method:
1. Write a design study, research/13-rust-dialect.md. For every v0-core item in 01's Tiers table, classify it under the dialect as: valid Rust as is; an attribute, library, or std replacement; a checker-only analysis; or impossible without changing rustc. Known hard cases: requires/ensures syntax, Pure, main(root: Root), overflow traps in release, Shared::with closures, scopes, simulator interception of std and blocking calls, deterministic HashMap, impl placement and module rules, FX diagnostics, the Bend boundary, and v1's evented runtime and field-borrow declarations.
2. For each path, estimate what must be built for the first demo (an agent-written concurrent service whose bug is found by seed and replayed exactly, and a PR that widens network authority flagged by the trust diff), plus ecosystem reach, the expected effect on E1 learnability, and what the thesis loses.
3. Cite prior art for the dialect path: lust, cap-std, capsec, cargo-cackle, Capslock, Prusti and Creusot attribute contracts, and loom, shuttle, turmoil, and madsim for deterministic simulation of Rust.
4. Run one adversarial review of the study (a second model preferred), written to reviews/.
5. Present a recommendation to the owner and record the decision in design/01-design.md (Thesis, Positioning, and D12/D13 as affected) and on this bead.
acceptance_criteria: research/13-rust-dialect.md exists with cited prior art and the per-feature classification of every v0-core item; an adversarial review of it is in reviews/ with each objection resolved or recorded; the owner's decision is recorded in design/01-design.md and on this bead. Cheapest falsifier: if D7, D15, or D11 cannot hold for safe code under the dialect without changing rustc, the dialect cannot carry the thesis and the new-language design stands.
close_reason: Owner adopted the checked Rust dialect as the v0 direction (D18, draft 3.6), gated by the feasibility spike fx-7qu; study research/15, review reviews/dialect-codex.md resolved.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Decision criteria from research/13-agent-fleets.md (2026-10-19): (1) per-spawn context tax: every fresh subagent pays the reference (about 19k tokens now), while Rust knowledge comes with the model, so measure the delta each path needs; (2) the check loop must hit D12's tens-of-milliseconds edit target, since fleets leave Rust over compile time (X7); (3) both paths must support sealed delegation boundaries and running an unreviewed branch's tests without a VM (beads filed alongside); (4) deterministic simulation with virtual time, so suites do not flake under parallel agents.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Concrete test case (owner, 2026-10-19): Eon (~/pjs/eon/eon, github.com/Yazelix/eon), a ~64k-line Rust workspace for long-running agent work: Orbit (terminal process server: PTYs, sessions, attach/detach), Venus (wgpu/Vulkan renderer), runtime and protocol crates, eon-manifest. Dependencies include wgpu, winit (Wayland), glyphon, accesskit, libghostty-vt (C), libc, serde/serde_json/toml (serde derive is a proc macro), arboard, wl-clipboard-rs; unsafe in about 10 files; almost no async. The study must answer for both paths: can Eon adopt Tide crate by crate, in what order (likely orbit-protocol and eon-workspace-protocol, then eon-manifest, then Orbit's core with a capability std), what blocks each crate (PTY/libc FFI, serde derives, C libraries), and what Orbit gains from deterministic simulation of attach, detach, and crash interleavings. Venus and windowing are expected to stay Rust. Also note the product fit: Eon could surface Tide's trust diff, replay seeds, and sealed boundaries per agent tab (research/13).

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Two more fleet needs from research/13 (P5, P7, P8), for both paths: every tide command bounded in time and output, with failures attributable to a change and seed ('Claude can't tell time'; agents disown broken builds); and a build cache safe for many concurrent agents across worktrees. The dialect path inherits Cargo's shared target/ lock, which blocks agents in separate worktrees (P15), so the study must say how a dialect avoids it.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Path correction (2026-10-19): the study goes in research/15-rust-dialect.md; research/13 is taken by 13-agent-fleets.md (and 14 by autoresearch). Read research/13 references in this bead as research/13-agent-fleets.md.

title: Define the staged Ferox symbol-record and symbol-graph rollout plan for the machine contract
description: The tooling specs now promise stable symbol identity, symbol records, and later symbol-graph data, but the queue does not yet track how those surfaces should be staged without overpromising during bootstrap. This task should define what symbol outputs appear first, what stability tier each belongs to, and what compiler prerequisites must exist before Ferox exposes richer symbol relationships.
design: Primary question: how should Ferox stage symbol-record and symbol-graph outputs so the machine contract is useful early without freezing unreliable semantics? Define: 1. the first symbol facts to expose; 2. the boundary between declaration records and richer graph edges; 3. stability tiers and versioning expectations; 4. dependencies on parsing, name resolution, package loading, and stable IDs; 5. non-goals for the bootstrap phase.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task clearly answers: what symbol data Ferox exposes first; what stays provisional; what graph edges are deferred; and what validation/diagnostic/logging expectations apply. Include staged output examples, rejected early overreach, and explicit prerequisites in the compiler pipeline.
notes: Additional revision after source-model audit: symbol-record and symbol-graph rollout should not stabilize source locations until the source-text/span contract is explicit, because byte spans, line/column data, and newline behavior are part of the public machine surface.
close_reason: Superseded: the owner discarded the first Ferox design (archived in archive/v0-design/) for the first-principles redesign in fx-agent-first-redesign-tf4; this work no longer applies.

title: Define the exact initial T074 Ferox grammar slice and parser recovery boundary
description: T074 currently names a small Ferox subset in broad terms, but the spec still exposes more syntax forms than the first parser should absorb. This task should define the exact initial grammar slice and recovery boundary for T074 so implementation proves parser shape without overcommitting grammar coverage too early.
design: Primary question: what exact syntax forms should the first real Ferox parser accept, reject, and recover around? Define the precise T074 grammar slice for declarations, statements, expressions, patterns, type syntax, comments/docs, and recovery boundaries. The goal is a deliberately small but coherent subset that matches the current source personality and formatter roadmap without pulling in deferred language systems.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task enumerates the exact T074 grammar surface, explicit exclusions, representative recovery scenarios, and the subset boundaries needed for parser tests, formatter work, and diagnostics snapshots. It should include examples of accepted files, rejected files, and partially recovered files, plus rationale for why omitted syntax stays out of the first slice.
notes: Decision: keep this planning bead and apply its outcome to T074 in v1 immediately. The exact initial parser slice should be: 1. file-level `////` docs, declaration `///` docs, and ordinary `//` comments preserved as trivia; 2. zero or more top-level `fn` declarations only, each with a name, explicit typed parameters, explicit `->` return type, and a block body; 3. statement forms limited to `let` / `let mut` with required initializer, optional local type annotation, simple assignment statements, `return`, and expression statements; 4. expression forms limited to name references, integer/string/bool literals, grouped expressions, block expressions, function calls, field access, a small binary operator set needed for basic examples, `if`/`else`, `match`, and postfix `?`; 5. type syntax limited to simple names and bracketed generic application such as `Option[T]` and `Result[T, E]`; 6. pattern syntax limited to `_`, name binding, simple literal patterns, unit-like names, tuple/variant patterns such as `some(value)` and `ok(value)`, plus tuple patterns. Explicit exclusions from T074: `async fn`, `await`, `pub`, `unsafe`, structs/enums/traits/use/module declarations, named-field struct/variant patterns, broad collection literals, float literal support, guards/or-patterns/alias patterns, destructuring `let`, and advanced type syntax. Recovery boundary: top-level recovery should sync on the next plausible `fn`; block recovery should sync on `;` or `}`; parameter and argument recovery should sync on `,` or closing delimiters; match-arm recovery should sync on `,` or `}`. Rationale: this is the smallest coherent slice that still exercises the Ferox source personality, `Option`/`Result` handling, formatter path, and structured diagnostics without pulling in deferred language systems. Apply in T074 now; later syntax growth should come from separate beads rather than expanding this bootstrap slice ad hoc.

title: Design sim.world.proc: child processes, signals and PTYs in the simulator
description:
## Why
Tide's simulator excludes signals and real child processes, which "need a sim.world.proc model" (design/03-authority-concurrency.md:2121-2125). Eon's recurring lifecycle races turn on spawn, exit and reap, SIGCHLD/SIGTERM, and PTY resize: the reap race eon-awmq.6, the startup deadline eon-l4e7s, and the lease and recovery bugs in supervisor.rs and sessions.rs. Seeded replay is what would catch them.

## Scope
Design note first, no code: sim.world.proc's surface (spawn, exit, wait/reap, signal delivery, PTY size), its determinism and fault model, how it relates to Proc and the real backend, and its tier. Item 2 of fx-vjvb's lease-race model is design input.

## Acceptance
A reviewed design note in design/03 (or a research/ report with recorded decisions) that names the surface, the determinism rules and the faults, and recommends a tier and follow-up beads.

Source: eon-desk proposal (/home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/eon-desk/tide-beads-from-eon.md) from an Opus assessment (tide-in-eon-report.md): use Eon as a reference workload; do not adopt Tide in Eon yet. Filed on Lucca's relayed approval (2026-11-12, via eon-desk): "if applicable, you can open beads in tide, so it can eventually serve eon better". Must not displace E1 or the first demo (fx-ic2, fx-nkv); Eon takes priority over Tide.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Coordinator decision, 2026-11-13 ~05:10Z, on candidate c1283ec (tide-fx-f6xp-work/report.md, research/30): accept all ten recommendations.
1. Tier: Later.
2. Opaque models behind Proc, no real children.
3. Owned event tables, embedded in REPLAY-1.
4. Per-Child wait ownership with cached status; no kill or reap on drop; signal death distinct from exit 143.
5. Coalesced hints plus subscriptions; one live subscription per signal; Child, Term, Kill, Winch, Hup; Kill cannot be subscribed to.
6. Command::spawn_pty(PtySize) -> (Child, Pty), one raw-mode PTY.
7. The existing scheduler and timers plus seeded model actions on a separate process RNG stream.
8. Six bounded fault families.
9. Children survive parent loss, subject to descriptor-closure effects; a node crash kills local processes.
10. Missing coverage is a D15 failure.
Reasons: each matches real POSIX semantics or keeps determinism without new source language, and Later protects E1 and the demo. Eon's need is met by fx-ayh2's scheduling, not by promoting the tier. Author to apply: mark 03 §9.9 decided; align 01's Later row and D15 with research/30 §9's text; add a Decision section to research/30. Then a Codex pass and an Opus round. fx-ayh2's refinement (research/30 §7) is applied by the coordinator when it lands.

title: Define the Ferox FP profile so it strengthens regularity and safety without increasing semantic entropy
description: Evaluate how far Ferox should lean into FP ideas such as ADTs, exhaustive matching, expression-oriented code, immutability-by-default, pipelines, and pure helper functions. The goal is to identify which FP influences strengthen Ferox's core thesis around safe change, low entropy, and agent-friendly tooling, and which FP directions would harm compile times, local reasoning, or systems-language coherence.
design: Current working hypothesis: restrained FP helps Ferox when it improves source-code regularity and local reasoning, but harms Ferox when it introduces major new semantic machinery. Likely good fits include ADTs, exhaustive matching, expression orientation, immutable-by-default style, and a narrow pipe operator. Likely bad fits include effect-heavy purity systems, monadic abstraction culture, operator proliferation, higher-kinded types, lazy defaults, and multiple equivalent composition idioms.
acceptance_criteria:
Produce a clear Ferox FP doctrine that explains:
1. Which FP ideas are core to the language identity.
2. Which are useful but secondary.
3. Which are out of scope because they would widen the core too much.
4. How the recommended FP profile interacts with ownership, async, tooling, compile times, and future verification.
5. Which canonical source examples demonstrate the doctrine in practice.

Also include a downstream implementation validation plan that covers:
- unit tests for parsing, lowering, formatting, and diagnostics of the accepted FP forms;
- golden/corpus tests for canonical examples and rejected anti-patterns;
- end-to-end scripts that exercise idiomatic transformation-heavy workflows;
- detailed logging/tracing expectations so failures in FP-related syntax, lowering, or formatting can be diagnosed quickly.

title: Differential trace runner: compare two revisions' event traces per seed
description:
## Why
Owner, 2026-11-17, agreeing with tide-lead's analysis of a tweet: "the most important devtool right now is the fast differential fuzzer/runner … run 2+ implementations and ensure that they always reach the same outcome & inspect their intermediate states".

Deterministic schedules make concurrent programs differentially testable. Two revisions that run the same seed see the same schedule, so any trace difference is real, not scheduling noise. That turns "replayable tests" into fearless concurrent refactors and optimizations. It's a stronger launch story than replay alone. Post-alpha (fx-qlek).

## Scope
- A driver mode, for example `tide-admit --tide-trace-diff OLD NEW`. The tide CLI (fx-a9oh) may wrap it later. It runs one #[sim_test] suite against two library revisions over the same explicit seed set, and compares their event traces per seed.
- Report per seed: identical, outcome-only difference, or trace divergence. For a divergence, name the first divergent event, with its index, kind and task, and some context from both sides.
- Allow a declared equivalence where traces may legitimately differ (e.g. ignore event kinds, or compare only sink output), recorded in the run's output.
- Reuse the NDJSON trace format and replay identity checks. The demo already compares trace hashes.
## Acceptance
- On the demo service: the fixed revision against itself is identical on every seed; buggy against fixed reports the first divergent event on each failing seed; a pure refactor of the fixed service (e.g. renaming a helper) is identical.
- Driver tests cover each verdict.
- GOVERNANCE.md Merge Rule.

title: Multi-file conformance cases for SEAL-2 and SEAL-3
description:
## Why

SEAL-2 and SEAL-3 (`design/04-contracts.md:1265-1330`) are v0 driver rules with no
conformance cases, because a case is one file and a seal needs a crate plus its
`tide.seal` (`conformance/rules.md:135-139`). fx-gcs cannot close until they have
cases (fx-gcs comment, 2026-10-21). The corpus is design work and needs no checker:
cases wait for the driver as other checker cases did.

## Evidence

- `conformance/rules.md:135-139`: SEAL-2 and SEAL-3 rows and the one-file limit.
- `conformance/README.md`: the case format and the runner's "awaiting the checker"
  listing.
- `design/04-contracts.md:1265-1318`: SEAL-2's interface, whole, test, and manifest
  entries; `:1319-1330`: SEAL-3's configurations, targets, and diagnostic parts;
  `:1369-1453`: the worked example.

## Scope

In scope: a multi-file case form in `conformance/` (a base package tree, the seal
taken from it with the writer fx-zr3 names, and one candidate edit with an
expected verdict: admitted, or FX0920 with its changed parts), the runner support to
list these cases, and cases for each SEAL-2 and SEAL-3 clause:
- interface entry: body edit admitted; signature, contract-use, or clause change and
  a changed body of a function a clause calls rejected; renaming a referenced helper
  admitted; a new impl or import that changes which item a sealed call selects
  rejected;
- whole function, whole type (an added `impl PartialEq`; a blanket impl that applies
  through `&T`; a changed associated type), and whole trait (a new impl admitted
  unless it applies to a type sealed whole);
- test entry: an edit to an unsealed function the test reaches rejected; an edit to a
  body behind an interface entry admitted; fewer seeds rejected;
- manifest entry: an added grant rejected;
- configurations and targets: a sealed `#[cfg(test)]` test not checked in the debug
  build; a build for a target the seal does not list rejected.

Out of scope: driver code; SEAL-4/5 (FX0921, `tide review`); rule changes.

## Acceptance

- Every SEAL-2 and SEAL-3 clause listed above has an admitted and a rejected case
  where both exist, with expected verdicts and parts.
- `conformance/run.sh` (or its Rust port, fx-upy) exits 0 and lists these cases as
  awaiting the checker; `conformance/rules.md` points SEAL-2 and SEAL-3 at them.

## Implementation Notes

1. Seal the base in the runner rather than committing hashes, so cases never hold
   stale hash bytes; the expected verdict names parts, not hashes.
2. Build on the runner fx-upy produces, so the multi-file form is written once.

## Verification

- `conformance/run.sh` exits 0 and its listing includes every new case.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if a SEAL-2 clause cannot be expressed as base plus edit; record it on fx-gcs.

title: Evaluate a functional-source, in-place-backend optimization direction for Ferox
description: Evaluate whether Ferox should deliberately target a backend strategy where transformation-friendly source code can compile to storage reuse or in-place updates when ownership and uniqueness prove that reuse is safe. The goal is to improve performance without polluting the surface language with mutation-heavy optimization idioms.
notes: Decision: Keep the idea only as a long-term backend optimization direction. Do not make functional-source/in-place-backend behavior part of the v1 or core v2 language promise. Revisit after the checked IR, ownership tracking, and first native backend are credible. Treat it as V3-or-later optimization and observability work, not as a surface-language feature.

title: Conformance corpus format, runner, and rule inventory
description:
## Why

The corpus children and the v0 checker's first slice share one case format and one runner. Pick
them once, before cases exist. Parent epic has the context.

## Evidence

- `design/01-design.md:143-147`: D0's conformance oracle, IDs traced to tests.
- `trials/e1-dialect/rustc/run.sh` and `trials/e1-dialect/rustc/std/`: a rustc oracle that type-
  and borrow-checks Rust 2024 crates against a stub Tide std injected as `std`. The runner should
  reuse this mechanism, not invent another.
- `spikes/d18/admit/tests/{pos,neg,pure,gate}`: the spike's admission cases, a shape to compare.
- About 83 rule IDs exist today, nearly all in 03 (SINK, LOCK, FFI, TASK, SEAL, RUST, RUN,
  GLOBAL, ROOT, PAR, ...); 02 has almost none.

## Scope

In scope:
- `conformance/`: the case format (one `.rs` file per case, with its rule IDs and expected
  verdict in a header comment, or a better shape if you find one), `conformance/run.sh`, and a
  trace table from rule ID to cases.
- Moving or copying the stub std into `conformance/` if the trial's copy must stay frozen as a
  record.
- A rule inventory: every v0-core normative rule in `design/02-memory.md`,
  `design/03-authority-concurrency.md`, and `design/04-contracts.md` that the checker or rustc
  decides, with its ID or `none yet`. An ID scheme for the rules that lack one, written into the
  chapter that owns them only if the scheme is decided here; assigning the IDs themselves is the
  sibling beads' work.
- About five seed cases that exercise every verdict kind.

Out of scope:
- Cases beyond the seeds (sibling beads).
- Runtime and sandbox tests.
- Any checker code.

## Acceptance

- `conformance/run.sh` exits 0 on the seed cases and reports, per case, PASS, FAIL, or AWAITS
  CHECKER (expected verdict is an `FX` code rustc cannot produce).
- A seed case whose expected verdict is wrong makes the runner exit nonzero.
- The format and the ID scheme are written down in `conformance/README.md`, and
  `design/01-design.md` D0 points to it.

## Verification

- `conformance/run.sh` exits 0; flipping one seed's expected verdict makes it exit nonzero.
- The runner and seeds finish through converge, then the review loop in `GOVERNANCE.md`.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if the stub-std mechanism cannot express a needed verdict; record why on the bead.
